isochrone:
Network isochrone

_Created 2026-10-14 · Updated 2026-10-14_

Draws the area reachable within a stated walking time along a street network, from one or more sites.

What you connect

PortWhat it expects
sitesthe points to walk from — pumps, clinics, depots
networka street network, from Street network

It produces polygons, one per site, which a map can draw and Summarize points in polygons can count into.

What you set

  • Minutes and metres per minute — together these are the distance budget.

5 minutes at 75 m/min is 375 m of street.

  • Corridor width — how wide a band to draw around the reachable streets.
  • Snap limit — how far a site may be from the nearest junction before the

run stops.

  • UTM zone and hemisphere — the projection it measures in. Every widget in a

workflow that measures must agree on this one, and the run is refused by name if they disagree.

What it assumes

A walk has three parts, and this charges for all three. From where you stand to the nearest junction; along the streets; from the last junction to the door. The region drawn is that whole route, buffered by the final leg.

  • The walk onto the network is measured — you can see it in the run evidence

as fw:networkSnaps — and deducted from your budget before any street is walked. On the Soho example that is 10.9 m of a 375 m budget. It is charged as a straight line at street speed, which is a lower bound on the real walk. Until 2026-10-14 it was free, and the catchment reached about 3% further than the minutes said.

  • The walk off the network, from the last junction to a doorway, is the

final walk off the street setting, and it is charged: it is that wide where the budget allows and narrower where it does not, so the region ends at its own time rather than 25 m beyond it. It assumes that ground can be walked, at street speed, which near the edge of the budget is where the catchment is most generous.

  • A site further than the snap limit from any mapped street is **routed

anyway**, with the straight line to the nearest junction charged against the budget. Its catchment carries fw:offNetworkMetres, the widget glows red and the Inspector names the leg. The line is a lower bound on that walk — it assumes you can cross whatever lies between — so the catchment reaches further than the ground allows. Before 2026-10-14 such a site stopped the run outright, taking every other site's catchment with it.

  • A site whose walk to the nearest street would spend the whole budget gets

no catchment at all. It reaches nothing in the stated time, which is the answer; there is no polygon, because the only shape available is a corridor-width disc around a junction the site cannot even get to. It is named in the alert and in fw:unconnectedSites, and the note on the result says the counts are over the sites that reached something.

Who this misleads, and in which direction

All of them push the same way: a poorly connected place looks better served than it is.

Streets and footpaths are mapped unevenly, and informal settlements least of all. Nothing is now excluded for being far from a street, but a site reached across an assumed straight line is still read as if that line were a footpath. Read a catchment over sparsely mapped ground as optimistic, check the widget's alert for sites routed off-network, and check fw:networkSnaps for how far each site had to go to reach a street.

What it is not

Not a service area, not a catchment anyone agreed to, and not a routed travel time. The corridor is an approximation of shape, drawn to be read, not measured.

Going deeper

The lab's snapping notebook measures the displacement on the example data. Experiment 114 records what would change it.
map_output:
Map

_Created 2026-10-14 · Updated 2026-10-14_

Draws what the workflow produced: boundaries, points, polygons, rasters and street networks, one layer over another.

What you connect

Ports receive or transmit. Layers are displayed. They do not correspond one to one, and the difference is the thing to understand about this widget.

PortWhat it expects
areaa study area, drawn as the ground the rest sits on
points … points_8point layers, one per connected source
polygonscatchments, hulls, cells or bands
contextpoints drawn beside polygons
rastera prepared or clipped raster
networka street network, drawn as itself
coveragea spatial coverage review

Which of these the node offers depends on its Input mode, and that is the part a practitioner meets as friction: a map in the default *spatial* mode draws the ports area, points, coverage and raster, and nothing else. Connect catchments to it and there is no port to aim at — not an error, nothing to drop onto. Change Input mode to *Catchment polygons / summaries* and the node redraws with a polygons port.

What it assumes

That a map is a map of one kind of thing. It is not, and the application works around its own assumption in three places: pointInputCount gives up to eight point layers, contextPoints gives one points layer beside polygons, and stack_polygons is an entire widget that collects up to six polygon layers into one value *ordered largest first so the smaller draw on top*. Each handles one type. None of them is allowed to say "layer".

Six of the ten maps in the shipped worked examples already draw more than one layer, and every one of the six gets there through one of those three.

That a layer which arrived at no port is not worth mentioning. The isochrone map has two ports and draws four layers — a boundary, four time bands, 250 death locations and eight pumps. The deaths were never wired to it: summarize_polygons keeps the points it counted on the value it returns, so they reach the map by travelling inside the polygons. The run evidence records this honestly — fw:layerCount 4, with fw:layerWithin "polygons" on the layer that has no port of its own — but nothing in the interface says it, and a reorder control listing the node's ports would not mention the layer you most want to move.

That the computation's roles are the map's emphasis. They are not. For a Voronoi catchment the pumps make the tessellation and the deaths are overlaid to show which catchment held the most; for an isochrone the pump and the network make the bands and the deaths are overlaid to show their distribution within them. In both, the pumps are the input and the deaths are the subject. The plot renderer draws sites red at radius 3.5 and observations gray at 2.7, so the thing each map exists to show is smaller and duller than the thing that produced the shape, and the legend reads *"Gray: observations · red: sites"*.

fw:layerRole records which is which, so a reader can see which way round a map was built. Nothing yet lets a practitioner set it.

What the run evidence records, and what it does not

Everything that changes the numbers is recorded as a term: corridorWidth, snapLimit, walkingSpeed, travelTime, travelDirection, fillInteriorHoles, metricCRS, countSemantics, the caveats each step stated, and — for the map itself — layerCount, layerKind, layerFeatureCount, layerRole, layerIndex, layerPort, layerWithin, mapLegend, mapBasemap, mapPresentation, the title, subtitle and source note.

Nothing records what changes the reading while leaving every number intact: there is no term for a layer's colour or size, for which layer the map is about, for what was cropped out of the frame, or for class breaks. A map can be read many ways and can be built to mislead, and this application's provenance would not catch it, because the provenance records computation and the misleading lives in presentation.

Who this misleads, and in which direction

A reader who takes visual weight as importance will read the pumps as the finding and the deaths as background, in both John Snow maps. That is the opposite of what each map was made to show.

What is not built

  • A map does not take layers of mixed types freely; it takes what its mode allows.
  • Draw order is the order the ports are declared, except inside stack_polygons, where it

is largest-area-first — a heuristic that suits nested bands and has no reason to suit a raster under points.

  • A practitioner cannot reorder layers, set a layer's role, or restyle one.
snap_to_network:
Snap to network

_Created 2026-10-14 · Updated 2026-10-14_

Moves each site to the nearest junction of a street network, so that steps which route along streets have somewhere to start.

What you connect

PortWhat it expects
sitesthe points to move
networka street network, from Street network

What it assumes

It moves your data. Every site comes out at a junction, not where it stood. How far each one travelled is measured and published as fw:greatestSnapDistanceMetres in the run evidence, and the output points are a derived dataset — they are not observations any more.

A site too far from the network is snapped anyway, and marked. Past the snap limit the point still moves to its nearest node, and carries offNetworkMetres as well as snapDistanceM — the first leg of its route crosses ground no street covers. The widget glows red on the canvas and the Inspector names each such site and the distance. What the limit decides is whether the point says so, not whether the site is in the result.

Nothing is dropped, and the widget refuses nothing on these grounds. Both of the earlier behaviours — an error before 2026-10-14, a silent omission for the hours after it — removed the places furthest from a mapped road, which is where street mapping is thinnest and where an access analysis is most often needed. The alert is the feedback loop instead: raise the limit, extend the network, or accept what is listed and say so in what you publish.

What to check

The snap distance, every time. If a site moved 200 m to reach a junction, then everything measured downstream starts 200 m from where it should, and that error does not appear anywhere in the final numbers.

Going deeper

The lab's snapping notebook checks the junction choice against pyproj and measures each displacement against a five-minute budget — one of the eight example pumps was decided by 0.43 m.
summarize_hull:
Observed extent (convex hull)

_Created 2026-10-14 · Updated 2026-10-14_

Draws the smallest convex outline containing your points, and measures the area it encloses.

What you connect

PortWhat it expects
pointsat least three located points

It produces one polygon carrying areaSquareMetres and spanMetres, which a rule or a table can read.

What it assumes

A hull is convex and your data may not be. Cases along a river, facilities along a coast — the hull fills in the space between them, so it asserts area where nothing was observed.

It is an outline of what was seen, not a boundary. Not a service area, not a catchment, not anything anyone agreed to. Where observation stopped is not where the thing being observed stopped.

Points without coordinates take no part, and the count that did is stated in the notes.

What to check

The span against the area. A hull far longer than it is wide is close to a line, and should be read as one — the widget says so in its notes when it happens.

Going deeper

The lab's hull notebook checks the outline and the area against Shapely.
